questions.question: A token bucket is full with capacity 120 and 170 requests arrive at once. Each request costs one token. How many can be admitted immediately?
options: It depends only on the refill rate
questions.explanation: Stored tokens bound the immediate burst. A full capacity-120 bucket can admit 120 one-token requests; the other 50 must be rejected or queued by a separate overflow policy.

questions.question: During a model interval, 900 requests are offered, 610 are allowed, and 90 remain queued. How many requests were rejected?
questions.explanation: The accounting invariant is offered = allowed + rejected + still queued. Therefore 900 - 610 - 90 = 200 rejected requests.

questions.question: Why can a fixed-window limit of 100 requests per minute admit nearly 200 requests in a short interval around a boundary?
options: The counter is not atomic
Requests can spend the end of one window and the beginning of the next
The refill rate doubles automatically
Every request is counted in two windows
questions.explanation: A client can use almost all 100 requests just before reset and another 100 just after reset. The implementation can be atomic and still have this boundary behavior.

questions.question: A centralized limiter becomes unreachable from one region. What is the primary risk of failing open for a sensitive write endpoint?
options: All healthy regions become slower because they must queue
The disconnected region can admit traffic without spending the authoritative budget
The global counter becomes more accurate
Legitimate traffic is guaranteed to be rejected
questions.explanation: Fail-open preserves availability by bypassing the unavailable decision, so the disconnected region can exceed the global allowance and expose the protected operation to abuse.

questions.question: Three regions each enforce an independent local limit of 600 requests per minute for the same identity. What is the naive global maximum?
options: 200 requests per minute
600 requests per minute
1,200 requests per minute
1,800 requests per minute
questions.explanation: Each independent region can spend 600, so the same identity can consume up to 3 x 600 = 1,800 requests per minute unless routing or budget allocation adds a global bound.

questions.question: What does a fail-closed leased regional limiter trade for bounded enforcement during a partition?
options: It removes the need for atomic local updates
It may reject legitimate traffic after the disconnected region exhausts its lease
It guarantees every region receives unlimited capacity
It makes the global coordinator part of every request path
questions.explanation: A lease lets the region continue only within a preallocated budget. Refusing requests after exhaustion bounds overshoot, but available global capacity elsewhere may be unusable until coordination returns.

questions.question: Why place the read, refill or expiry calculation, comparison, and counter update in one Redis Lua script?
options: To make the operation atomic against concurrent limit checks
To replicate the key to every region synchronously
To guarantee Redis can never fail
To avoid choosing a stable identity key
questions.explanation: A single script prevents concurrent gateways from reading the same old allowance and both spending it. Atomicity protects one Redis owner; cross-region availability and failover policy remain separate decisions.
